lecture_title: What Creativity Is, and Why Your Ideas Get Stuck
content:
First meeting of the semester. Two jobs: make the room safe enough to say a bad idea out loud, and get every student committed to one real enterprise they will work on for fifteen weeks.

THE CORE DISTINCTION
Creativity is having ideas. Innovation is an idea that actually reaches somebody. A tea stall owner inventing a new masala is creativity; forty people a day buying it and coming back is innovation. One is private, the other changed something for someone. This course is about getting from the first to the second.

WHERE IDEAS DIE
Between 'I thought of it' and 'someone used it' there is a long gap in which most ideas quietly disappear. The semester is spent in that gap.

FOUR BARRIERS, NONE OF THEM ABOUT TALENT
1. Judging too early - killing an idea before it is finished.
2. Fear of looking foolish in front of people you know.
3. 'We have always done it this way.'
4. The expertise trap - knowing so well how a thing is done that you cannot see it done differently.
Because these are predictable they are beatable, and each has a technique against it. Mind mapping (Unit 2) works on the second and third; SCAMPER (Unit 3) works on the fourth; the warm-up in this session works on the first.

THE ANCHOR ENTERPRISE
Each student selects one real local enterprise in this session and carries it through all three units. Selection criterion stated plainly to students: not the most interesting business, but the one whose owner will actually answer the phone.

TWENTY QUESTIONS
Students write twenty questions for their owner - questions, not answers. Twenty is deliberately more than is comfortable: the first eight are obvious, the next seven are effortful, and the last five are where the interesting ones live. Pairs then sharpen each other's lists, circling three and striking five.

learning_objectives.statement: Define creativity and distinguish it from innovation in a business context.
Explain why most ideas fail between conception and implementation.
Identify the four common barriers to creativity and recognise them in their own thinking.
Select a real local enterprise as a semester-long anchor and justify the choice on access rather than interest.
Generate twenty investigative questions for an enterprise owner, prioritising quantity over polish.

active_learning_components.desc: Silent, written, never read aloud: the last time you had an idea and did not say it — what stopped you? Primes the barrier theme with the student's own evidence. From Session 2 this slot is retrieval practice.
active_learning_components.rationale: No prior session to retrieve, so the slot primes instead.

active_learning_components.desc: Teams of four generate the worst possible ideas for a familiar prompt, then invert their worst one. First public act of the semester is deliberately being wrong.
Students choose their semester-long anchor enterprise and complete sections 1 and 2 of templates/anchor_business_brief.md from existing knowledge. Blanks expected.
Each student writes twenty questions they would need to ask their anchor's owner. Questions, not answers; quantity over polish.
Pairs exchange briefs; each partner circles the three sharpest questions, strikes the five weakest, and explains both choices aloud.

Shortened two-minute team-attributed pitch (weeks 1-2 rule): who is this business and what is the sharpest question we found. One critique round using templates/peer_critique_protocol.md, with the facilitator modelling the first full set of moves. Attainment beat for CO 109.2.
Silent completion of the Session 1 page of templates/idea_log.md. Box 4 is the entry students revisit in the week-15 look-back.

between_sessions: Visit or phone the anchor enterprise and ask the three sharpest questions. Bring the answers, in any language, to Session 2.

forward_link.say: The twenty-questions habit is the move you will use when you open a case for the first time. A case is just a business whose owner is not in the room to answer you.

early_finisher_extension: Write questions 21 to 30. The good ones are hiding after twenty.
